Zymera — Team Coverage, in Plain Terms

Project Zymera · plain-language summary

A robot team that explores unknown ground — together

Cover as much of a map as possible, while staying within radio range of each other, in a place none of them has seen before.

A short tour of where things stand. Every section links to its full, interactive version at the bottom.

1The job

A handful of robots are dropped into an obstacle-filled map. Each one sees only the square right around it, and can talk only to teammates that are close enough. Working from those scraps, the team has to spread out and cover the whole area — without the group drifting so far apart that it loses contact.

2What it looks like

Green = ground covered · dark = wall · dots = robots · faint ring = radio range · dashed line = an active radio link.

Two things — and only two — decide how well it goes: the environment (wide-open ground is easy; tight walled rooms trap the team at about half the map) and how big the team is versus the map (a bigger team on a bigger map covers a smaller share). Everything else we tried barely moved the result.

3The reward — exact

Every step, each robot i gets a score it learns (by trial and error) to maximize. In words: +3 per new patch covered, +2 per teammate still reachable, −4 for piling onto an occupied cell. Written out exactly (ctde_v0/env_utils.compose_reward):

ri = 3·covi  +  2·reachi  −  4·colli  −  1·[ λ · max(0, τ − λ₂) ]
  • covi = new_coverage — cells newly covered by the team this step, credited to i.  weight w_coverage = 3
  • reachi = reach_fraction — fraction of the other N−1 robots that i can reach over the comm graph.  weight w_connectivity = 2
  • colli = collisions — teammates sharing i's cell.  weight w_collision = −4
  • penalty = soft_lambda_penalty(=1) · [ dual λ · max(0, τ − λ₂) ] — the connectivity shortfall; λ₂ = team's true Fiedler value (connection strength), τ ∈ (0.5, 0.7) = the floor. Identically 0 in every run (λ₂ ≈ 2 > τ ⟹ shortfall 0).

Off in these runs (weight 0 / not applied): the connectivity-floor "barrier", an anti-overlap term, a congestion price, an info-gain bonus.

4The loss — exact

The reward drives a standard actor–critic update (PPO). Each step's advantage (how much better an action did than expected) is estimated with GAE, then standardized per minibatch:

δt = rt + γ·Vt+1 − Vt  ;  Ât = δt + γλ·Ât+1  ;  Â ← (Â − mean Â)/(std Â + ε)   [ γ = 0.99, λ = 0.95 ]

Training then minimizes the total loss (ctde_v0/ppo.loss):

L = Lpolicy  +  0.5·Lvalue  +  0.1·Laux  +  0.001·Ldegree  −  0.01·H
  • Lpolicy = clipped policy-gradient on the move + role heads:  −mean( min(ρ·Â, clip(ρ, 0.8, 1.2)·Â) ),  ρ = πnew/πold, clip ε = 0.2
  • 0.5·Lvalue = mean( (V − return)² ) — the critic's squared prediction error.  vf_coef = 0.5
  • 0.1·Laux = mean( (λ̂₂ − λ₂)² ) — each robot predicting the team's connection strength from its own view (the self-awareness head).  aux_beta = 0.1
  • 0.001·Ldegree = Varbatch( mean-comm-degree ) — penalizes drift in average neighbor count.  degree_reg = 1e-3
  • − 0.01·H = entropy bonus on move + role choices (keeps exploration alive).  entropy_coef = 0.01

The connectivity controller sets the dial λ from the batch shortfall v = max(0, τ − mean λ₂), three variants:

soft: λ = const  ·  lagrangian: λ ← max(0, λ + 0.05·v)  ·  PID: λ = max(0, 1.0·v + 0.01·Σv + 0.1·(v − vprev))

Because λ₂ ≈ 2 never drops below τ = 0.5–0.7, the shortfall v = 0, so λ stays 0 for all three and the reward's penalty term vanishes — that is exactly why the three controllers came out indistinguishable.

Optimizer: AdamW (lr 3e-4) + global-norm gradient clip at 0.5. Per update: 6 PPO epochs × 4 minibatches, over 16 parallel rollouts × 100 steps.

5What each robot actually knows

Each robot starts blind — one square of the map — and fills the rest in as it moves and hears from neighbors. Everything it knows is squeezed into a 64-number internal summary that drives its decisions.

We opened that summary up to check it's real: you can read a robot's true position, how much it has covered, and how spread out the team is straight back out of those 64 numbers — so its internal picture faithfully matches reality. One surprise: once the team is large, radio-sharing adds little to what any single robot can read out — its own sensing already carries most of it.

6The connectivity result

The headline experiment compared three connectivity controllers — three different ways of turning that dial. As section 4 explains, the dial never left zero, so all three behaved identically. We confirmed it across two team sizes and many repeats: no measurable difference. The connectivity knob is a switch that's never flipped — the real levers are the environment and the team-vs-map size from section 2.

7Still in progress

Personalities — can identical robots be given slightly different "temperaments" when deployed, so they naturally split the work instead of clumping? Early days.   Convergence — watching how the long training runs settle down over time. Ongoing.
